children: wrap itself around Hugging Face? There’s no obvious return from spending $12.9 billion for the AI platform, which allows developers to share tools, models and data sets. If Jensen Huang, the founder and CEO of the $5.5 trillion chipmaker, wants to experiment and spend a measly 0.2% of the company’s market value on an acquisition, that’s fine. He's earned the leeway, considering his track record. It also looks like a cheap form of insurance.

Nvidia is emphatic it won't close up Hugging Face or push developers toward its own hardware or services. Such assurances should always be taken with a grain of salt, but there is a reason to suspect it’s true. A thriving open-source community is perhaps the best way to ensure machine learning is omnipresent, because it provides models that are customizable and cheap. In a call explaining the deal, the company talked about how it is a big proponent of everyone around the world building out AI infrastructure. That would, after all, mean many more data centers are built, perhaps stocked with Nvidia gear.
The rationale echos past tech deals. For instance, Alphabet's

acquisition of Android in 2005. The goal wasn’t to make money from licensing out the phone operating system, but to ensure people kept using Google search, and prevent Apple from dominating smart phones and establishing its own service. It worked; the company claims over 95% of mobile search according to StatCounter.

Nvidia’s interest is in having a broad customer base. Having one primary firm, whether it’s OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or someone else, would be dangerous. A buyer with huge market share has more negotiating leverage on chip prices. These companies are also developing their own data center gear, and the bigger they are, the more resources and incentive they have to cut out Nvidia.

Of course, who knows where the AI market will go in months, let alone years. So there’s a certain unreality about what possible insurance might be worth. Perhaps that’s best seen in the $12,930,300,000 price tag. Sure, a leading platform, especially one in the headlines after rogue OpenAI agents attacked it, has merit in tech. But the Unicode for the hugging face emoji, converted to decimal, also yields the number 129,303. The deal might make strategic sense, but it’s a warning bell of hubris if the value of money in AI seems increasingly arbitrary.

Nvidia said on September 3 that it had agreed to buy Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. The target is an open platform where AI developers share tools, models and data sets. Nvidia said Hugging Face will remain an open platform and that Nvidia compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face.
Under the deal, Nvidia will pay $11.9 billion to Hugging Face investors, and offer up to $1 billion in equity-based retention to ​employees who join Nvidia.
